claims.statement: Tom Allen conducted the Champions' Rest, a combined saloon and concert hall.
J. W. L. Gillespie recently acquired the Champion's Rest, a concert hall and saloon on Market Street, formerly owned by Tom Allen.
A bill of sale for the Champion's Rest was given to J. W. L. Gillespie on Monday evening, March 30, 1903.
Mrs. Hartgrove, according to Mrs. Taylor, had assumed power of attorney and took charge of the money in the cash register at the saloon.
The Hyde Park brewery placed Gillespie, proprietor of a saloon on North Broadway, in charge of Allen's saloon; he took hold on Monday, March 30, 1903.
J. W. L. Gillespie said he had a bill of sale for the saloon; in the dispute at the saloon that followed, guns were drawn, but Murphy remained in charge.
Mrs. Hartgrove had charge of the saloon, The Champion's Rest, during Allen's illness and was said to have a bill of sale for it.
Persons with a bill of sale held the living rooms over the saloon, and an agent of Allen's daughter had charge of the bar.
Bartender John Murphy pointed a revolver at W. J. Gillespie when he entered the saloon with William Burns, telling them he was running the Champion's Rest.
Gillespie had paid $125 rent for Allen's saloon, starting April 1, and had installed William Burns and his family in Allen's apartments above it to manage the place.
On April 2, 1903, John Murphy, the bartender, met J. W. L. Gillespie with a revolver at the Champion's Rest when Gillespie tried to take possession.
On April 2, 1903, J. W. L. Gillespie was driven from the saloon at the muzzle of a revolver when he tried to take possession.
John Murphy acted on the advice of Robert Lyons, Allen's bartender for sixteen years, on the night of April 2, 1903.
J. W. L. Gillespie tried to take possession of Allen's saloon at 619 Market Street with a bill of sale made by Allen, who was sick and unable to run the business.
The bartender, Murphy, admitted he had the day's receipts but refused to hand them over to anyone except Allen.
On April 3, 1903, Gillespie came from Allen's room with an attorney and a notary, carrying a second bill of sale bearing Allen's mark.
The night after Allen's death, a yard of crape hung from the doorknob of his saloon, Tom Allen's Champion's Rest, at 619 Market street, which was dark inside.
W. A. Byrne, acting for J. W. L. Gillespie, claims a bill of sale for the goods and fixtures of the Champion's Rest.
W. A. Byrne said he was prepared to hold the upstairs rooms of the Champion's Rest by force of arms if necessary.
John Murphy, Allen's bartender for several years, refuses to give up possession of the saloon until the matter is straightened out.
After Allen's death, W. A. Byrne, representing J. W. L. Gillespie, held the living rooms over the Champion's Rest at 619 Market street and declared he would keep them.
John Murphy, Allen's old bartender, was said to be holding the barroom in the interest of Allen's daughter, Mrs. Mary Taylor, of 3427 Clark Avenue (printed %427).
As of April 1903 The Champion's Rest was the headquarters of the Albion Social Club and was known as a resort for the city's poor with no place to sleep.
Tom Allen's saloon was on Market near Seventh street in St. Louis, and the estate inventory listed the old piano used at concerts there.
The Champion's Rest, once owned by Tom Allen, is now run by Jack Gillespie, a Klondike fortune-seeker.
At the Champion's Rest a hobo may sleep in a chair in the parquet even if he has no money.
